title: General properties of activation functions
prompt: Which statement about activation functions is correct?

options.text: They typically operate component-wise on tensors.
options.explanation: Common activations such as ReLU, sigmoid and tanh apply the same scalar function independently to every element of the tensor, so the output has the same shape as the input.

options.text: Every activation function has trainable parameters.
options.explanation: Most standard activations (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) are fixed functions with no parameters. Only some variants, such as PReLU with its learnable slope, have trainable parameters.

options.text: All activation functions must be monotone.
options.explanation: Nothing requires monotonicity; it is only required that the function is non-linear. For example $x\cdot\text{sigmoid}(x)$ (SiLU) dips below zero for negative inputs and then rises again, so it is not monotone.

options.text: Maxout is a standard one-input/one-output activation.
options.explanation: Maxout takes the maximum over several candidate outputs of different linear maps, so it needs several inputs per unit and extra weights. It is not a scalar-to-scalar function like ReLU.

hints: Think of ReLU, sigmoid and tanh: do they have weights? What shape does their output have?
Name one activation that has a parameter and one that is not monotone.
explanation: An activation function is a non-linearity that is usually applied element by element to the output of a linear layer, so the tensor shape is preserved. It does not need parameters (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh have none) and does not need to be monotone. Exceptions exist (PReLU has a learnable slope, Softmax and Maxout combine several components), which is why the word 'typically' matters.

title: Identify the sigmoid formula
prompt: Which formula defines the sigmoid activation function?

options.text: $\exp(x_i)/\sum_{j}\exp(x_{j})$
options.explanation: This is Softmax: each component is exponentiated and divided by the sum over all components. Sigmoid acts on a single scalar and has no sum over other components.
This is ReLU, which is piecewise linear and unbounded above, whereas sigmoid is smooth and bounded in (0, 1).
This is the softsign function. It looks similar (an S-shape) but its range is (-1, 1) and it approaches its limits only polynomially, not exponentially.
This is the logistic sigmoid: it equals 0.5 at $x=0$, tends to 1 as $x\to\infty$ and to 0 as $x\to-\infty$.
This is a rescaled sigmoid that equals $\tanh(x)$, with range (-1, 1). It is sigmoid-shaped, but it is the tanh activation, not the sigmoid.

hints: Sigmoid squashes any real number into (0, 1) and equals 0.5 at zero.
Check the value of each formula at $x=0$.
explanation: The sigmoid is $\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$. At $x=0$ it equals 0.5 and it is bounded in (0, 1). Several other formulas are easily confused with it: Softmax (a vector function with a sum in the denominator), ReLU, softsign and tanh (which equals $2\sigma(2x)-1$ and is centred at 0).

title: Properties of the sigmoid
prompt: Which statements about sigmoid are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Sigmoid is a smooth activation function.
options.explanation: $\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})$ is infinitely differentiable everywhere, with derivative $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$.

options.text: It has a trainable slope parameter by default.
options.explanation: The standard sigmoid is a fixed function with no parameters. A learnable slope is the idea behind variants like PReLU, not the sigmoid.

options.text: Its output is zero-centered.
options.explanation: Sigmoid outputs are always positive, in (0, 1), with average around 0.5. Tanh is the zero-centred relative. Non-centred outputs make the inputs of the next layer all positive, which can slow optimisation.

options.text: It cannot saturate.
options.explanation: For large $|x|$ the output flattens at 0 or 1 and the derivative $\sigma(1-\sigma)$ goes to 0. This saturation is the well-known weakness of sigmoid.

options.text: Its output is bounded between 0 and 1.
options.explanation: As $x\to\infty$ the output tends to 1 and as $x\to-\infty$ it tends to 0, so the output always lies in (0, 1), which is why it is used for probabilities.

hints: Evaluate sigmoid at very large positive and negative inputs.
What is the sign of every sigmoid output?
explanation: Sigmoid is smooth, parameter-free and bounded in (0, 1). Because its outputs are all positive it is not zero-centred, and because it flattens out for large $|x|$ it saturates, so its gradient vanishes there. Remember these two drawbacks, since tanh and ReLU-type functions were introduced largely to address them.

title: What saturation does to gradients
prompt: Which statement best describes sigmoid saturation?

options.text: Far from zero, the sigmoid derivative always becomes larger.
options.explanation: The derivative $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$ is largest (0.25) at $x=0$ and shrinks towards 0 as $|x|$ grows, so it becomes smaller, not larger.

options.text: Saturation guarantees faster learning.
options.explanation: Near-zero derivatives mean near-zero weight updates for the affected units, so learning slows down or stalls. Nothing about saturation speeds training.

options.text: Far from zero, the sigmoid derivative can become very small and impede backpropagation.
options.explanation: In the flat regions the local gradient is close to 0, and backpropagation multiplies by it, so the gradient reaching earlier layers vanishes.

options.text: Saturation makes sigmoid outputs zero-centered.
options.explanation: Saturated outputs are close to 0 or 1 and never negative, so the outputs stay non-zero-centred. Centring is a separate property that tanh has and sigmoid lacks.

hints: Write the derivative $\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$ and evaluate it at $x=10$.
Backpropagation multiplies local derivatives along the chain.
explanation: When $|x|$ is large, $\sigma(x)$ is close to 0 or 1, so $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))\approx 0$. The upstream gradient is multiplied by this tiny factor, so very little signal flows back to earlier layers (vanishing gradient). Since the derivative is at most 0.25, stacking many sigmoid layers shrinks gradients even without saturation.

title: Properties of tanh
prompt: Which statements about tanh are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Its output lies in $[0, +\infty)$.
options.explanation: That range describes ReLU-like functions. Tanh takes negative values for negative inputs and is bounded above by 1.

options.text: It never saturates.
options.explanation: Tanh flattens to -1 and 1 for large $|x|$, where its derivative $1-\tanh^2(x)$ goes to 0. It saturates just like sigmoid.

options.text: Its output is zero-centered.
options.explanation: Tanh is an odd function ($\tanh(-x)=-\tanh(x)$) with $\tanh(0)=0$, so its outputs are symmetric around 0.

options.text: It is not zero-centered.
options.explanation: This contradicts the symmetry of tanh: it is odd and passes through the origin. The non-zero-centred function is sigmoid (outputs in (0, 1)).

options.text: Its output is bounded between -1 and 1.
options.explanation: $\tanh(x)=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}$ tends to 1 as $x\to\infty$ and to -1 as $x\to-\infty$, so the output stays in (-1, 1).

hints: Compare tanh with a rescaled sigmoid: $\tanh(x)=2\sigma(2x)-1$.
Is tanh(-2) equal to -tanh(2)?
explanation: Tanh is a zero-centred, odd, S-shaped function bounded in (-1, 1). It fixes the non-centred outputs of sigmoid, but it still saturates for large $|x|$, so vanishing gradients remain a problem in deep stacks.

title: Identify the ReLU formula
prompt: Which formula defines ReLU?

options.text: $x\cdot\text{sigmoid}(x)$
options.explanation: This is SiLU (also called Swish), a smooth activation that is slightly negative for negative inputs. It is not ReLU.

options.text: $\log(1+\exp(x))$
options.explanation: This is Softplus, a smooth approximation of ReLU that is strictly positive everywhere. ReLU itself has an exact zero region and a kink at 0.
This is ReLU6, which additionally clamps large values to 6. Plain ReLU has no upper bound.
ReLU passes positive inputs unchanged and sets negative inputs to 0.

hints: ReLU stands for Rectified Linear Unit: linear for positive inputs, zero otherwise.
Which formula has no upper bound and no smooth part?
explanation: ReLU is $\max(0,x)$: identity for $x>0$ and zero for $x\le 0$. The other formulas are related activations: SiLU multiplies by a sigmoid gate, Softplus is its smooth version, and ReLU6 adds an upper clamp.

title: A fact about ReLU
prompt: Which statement about ReLU is correct?

options.text: ReLU requires a learnable slope parameter.
options.explanation: ReLU is the parameter-free function $\max(0,x)$. A learnable slope belongs to PReLU.

options.text: A ReLU unit can die if it never activates, causing its gradient to remain zero.
options.explanation: If a unit's pre-activation is negative for every input, its output and gradient are 0, so its incoming weights never get updated and it stays inactive (the dying ReLU problem).

options.text: ReLU outputs are bounded above by 1.
options.explanation: For positive inputs ReLU is the identity, so outputs are unbounded above. A bound of 1 would be a property of sigmoid or Hardtanh.

options.text: ReLU has a nonzero gradient for every negative input.
options.explanation: For $x<0$ the output is constantly 0, so the gradient is exactly 0. Variants like Leaky ReLU were introduced precisely to give negative inputs a small nonzero gradient.

hints: What is the derivative of $\max(0,x)$ for $x<0$?
If the gradient is always zero for a unit, can its weights change?
explanation: ReLU has gradient 1 for $x>0$ and 0 for $x<0$. A unit whose pre-activation is negative on all data (for example after a large update or a bad bias) receives no gradient and can never recover; it is 'dead'. Leaky ReLU, PReLU and ELU address this by keeping some gradient on the negative side.

title: Main idea of Leaky ReLU
prompt: What is the main idea of Leaky ReLU?

options.text: Use a small nonzero slope for negative inputs.
options.explanation: Leaky ReLU is $x$ for $x>0$ and $0.01x$ (a small fixed slope) for $x<0$, so a gradient still flows through negative inputs.

options.text: Use a learnable negative slope by default.
options.explanation: A learned negative slope is PReLU. Leaky ReLU's slope is a fixed hyperparameter (0.01 by default in PyTorch).

options.text: Take the maximum over multiple candidate neurons.
options.explanation: That describes Maxout, which takes the max over several linear candidates; Leaky ReLU is a single element-wise function.

options.text: Clamp all positive outputs to 1.
options.explanation: Leaky ReLU is the identity for positive inputs. Clamping the positive side would be a Hardtanh-style or ReLU6-style behaviour.

options.text: Randomly sample the negative-side slope from a fixed interval during training.
options.explanation: That is RReLU (randomized leaky ReLU). Leaky ReLU uses one fixed slope that does not change during training.

hints: The 'leak' refers to what happens for negative inputs.
Which variants learn or randomise the slope, and which keep it fixed?
explanation: Leaky ReLU fixes the dying-ReLU problem with a tiny constant slope $a$ on the negative side: $f(x)=\max(0,x)+a\min(0,x)$. Related variants differ only in how $a$ is chosen: fixed (Leaky ReLU), learned (PReLU) or randomly sampled in training (RReLU).

title: PReLU compared with Leaky ReLU
prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes PReLU from Leaky ReLU?

options.text: Both PReLU and Leaky ReLU always use a zero slope for negative inputs.
options.explanation: A zero slope on the negative side is plain ReLU. Both PReLU and Leaky ReLU exist precisely to use a nonzero negative slope.

options.text: PyTorch recommends weight decay on the PReLU slope parameter.
options.explanation: The PyTorch documentation warns against weight decay on the PReLU slope, because decay pulls the slope towards 0 and turns the unit back into a plain ReLU.

options.text: PReLU learns the negative-side slope, whereas Leaky ReLU uses a fixed slope.
options.explanation: PReLU treats the slope $a$ as a trainable parameter (one per channel or one shared), while Leaky ReLU keeps it as a fixed hyperparameter.

options.text: PReLU has no parameters, whereas Leaky ReLU learns its slope.
options.explanation: This reverses the two: PReLU is the one with a trainable parameter, and Leaky ReLU has a fixed slope.

hints: The 'P' in PReLU stands for 'parametric'.
Which of the two adds trainable parameters to the model?
explanation: Both functions are $x$ for $x>0$ and $a\,x$ for $x<0$. The only difference is $a$: a fixed small constant in Leaky ReLU and a trainable parameter in PReLU. Because the learned slope is a parameter, PReLU slightly increases the parameter count, and weight decay on it is discouraged.

title: What ReLU6 does
prompt: What does ReLU6 do?

options.text: It computes the maximum over six channels.
options.explanation: The '6' is a clipping value, not a number of channels. Maximising over groups of inputs is the Maxout idea.

options.text: It maps all inputs to [-1, 1].
options.explanation: ReLU6 never outputs negative values; its range is [0, 6]. A [-1, 1] range belongs to tanh or Hardtanh.

options.text: It applies ReLU and clamps large values to 6.
options.explanation: $\text{ReLU6}(x)=\min(\max(0,x),6)$: zero for negatives, identity on [0, 6], and constant 6 beyond that.

options.text: It is identical to Leaky ReLU with slope 6.
options.explanation: Leaky ReLU has a small slope for negative inputs, whereas ReLU6 is exactly 0 there. Its slope is 1 on [0, 6], not 6.

options.text: It linearly rescales all positive ReLU outputs into the interval [0, 6].
options.explanation: ReLU6 does not rescale: values between 0 and 6 pass through unchanged and only larger values are cut off at 6. A rescaling would change the slope on the positive side.

hints: Write the formula as a combination of max and min.
What is ReLU6(3), and what is ReLU6(10)?
explanation: ReLU6 is $\min(\max(0,x),6)$: ReLU with an upper clamp at 6. It is the identity for inputs in [0, 6] and saturates outside, which bounds the activations (useful e.g. in low-precision networks). The key point is that it clips rather than rescales.

title: A fact about ELU
prompt: Which statement about ELU is correct?

options.text: It always outputs only nonnegative values.
options.explanation: For $x<0$, ELU gives $\alpha(e^x-1)$, which is negative and approaches $-\alpha$. Negative outputs help push the mean activation towards zero.

options.text: Its alpha parameter is learnable by default.
options.explanation: In ELU, $\alpha$ is a fixed hyperparameter (default 1.0). It is not trained.

options.text: It is exactly the same as ReLU6.
options.explanation: ReLU6 clamps to [0, 6] and is piecewise linear, while ELU is unbounded above on the positive side and uses an exponential on the negative side.

options.text: For negative inputs it uses an exponential form controlled by alpha.
options.explanation: ELU is $x$ for $x>0$ and $\alpha(\exp(x)-1)$ for $x\le 0$; $\alpha$ sets the value $-\alpha$ to which the negative side saturates.

hints: Evaluate ELU at a large negative input.
Is alpha a weight or a hyperparameter?
explanation: ELU is the identity for positive inputs and $\alpha(e^x-1)$ for negative inputs, so it is smooth-ish, has nonzero gradient for negative $x$ and negative outputs bounded below by $-\alpha$. $\alpha$ is fixed by the user, not learned.

title: Properties of Maxout
prompt: Which statements about Maxout are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It computes multiple candidate outputs and returns their maximum.
options.explanation: A Maxout unit computes $k$ affine functions $w_i^\top x+b_i$ of its input and outputs the largest one.

options.text: Using k candidate values requires k times as many weights as one candidate.
options.explanation: Each of the $k$ candidates has its own weight vector and bias, so a Maxout layer has $k$ times the parameters of the corresponding single-candidate layer.

options.text: It averages the candidate outputs rather than taking a maximum.
options.explanation: Maxout takes the maximum. An average of affine functions would just be another affine function, adding no non-linearity.

options.text: It is identical to spatial max pooling.
options.explanation: Max pooling has no weights and takes the max over spatial neighbours of the same feature. Maxout takes the max over several separately learned linear transformations of the input.

options.text: It never changes the parameter count.
options.explanation: The extra candidates need extra weights, so the parameter count grows by a factor of $k$ compared with a layer producing one candidate per unit.

hints: How many weight vectors does a unit with k candidates need?
Is an average of linear functions still non-linear?
explanation: Maxout replaces a fixed non-linearity with a learnable piecewise-linear function: the max over $k$ linear maps. This makes it very flexible but multiplies the weights of the layer by $k$. It differs from pooling, which has no parameters, and from an average, which would remain linear.

title: Properties of Softplus
prompt: Which statements about Softplus are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It is non-differentiable at zero.
options.explanation: Softplus, $\log(1+e^x)$, is smooth everywhere and its derivative is the sigmoid. It is ReLU that has a kink at 0.

options.text: Its output is always negative.
options.explanation: Since $1+e^x>1$, the logarithm is positive for every $x$. At $x=0$ the value is $\log 2\approx 0.693$.

options.text: It is a smooth approximation of ReLU.
options.explanation: For large positive $x$, $\log(1+e^x)\approx x$, and for large negative $x$ it tends to 0, so it follows $\max(0,x)$ with the corner smoothed out.

options.text: Its output is always positive.
options.explanation: Because $e^x>0$, we have $1+e^x>1$ and $\log(1+e^x)>0$ for all $x$, although it approaches 0 for very negative inputs.

options.text: It is identical to Hardshrink.
options.explanation: Hardshrink is a piecewise function that sets values within $[-\lambda,\lambda]$ to 0 and leaves others unchanged. It is not smooth and not positive.

hints: Compute Softplus at x = 0, at a large positive x and at a large negative x.
Which function's derivative is the sigmoid?
explanation: Softplus $=\log(1+e^x)$ is a strictly positive, infinitely differentiable curve that approaches 0 on the left and the line $y=x$ on the right, i.e. a smoothed ReLU. Its derivative is the sigmoid, so unlike ReLU it has no kink at zero.

title: Properties of Softmax
prompt: Which statement about Softmax is correct?

options.text: Its output can be arbitrarily negative.
options.explanation: Softmax outputs are $e^{x_i}/\sum_j e^{x_j}>0$, so every output lies in (0, 1). Negative values arise in LogSoftmax, not in Softmax.

options.text: It is applied independently to each scalar with no interaction among components.
options.explanation: Every output depends on all inputs through the shared denominator $\sum_j e^{x_j}$. Raising one score lowers all other probabilities.

options.text: It is identical to LogSoftmax.
options.explanation: LogSoftmax is the logarithm of the Softmax output. The two differ in range: (0, 1) for Softmax and $(-\infty, 0)$ for LogSoftmax.

options.text: Its outputs are nonnegative and sum to 1 across the normalized components.
options.explanation: Each output is positive and dividing by the sum of all exponentials makes them add to exactly 1, so they can be read as a probability distribution.

hints: Write the formula and look at the denominator.
What is the sum of the outputs over the normalised dimension?
explanation: Softmax, $\text{softmax}(x)_i=e^{x_i}/\sum_j e^{x_j}$, maps a vector of scores to a probability distribution over the normalised dimension. Because of the shared denominator the components interact, which is what distinguishes it from element-wise activations.

title: Why LogSoftmax is a fused operation
prompt: Why is LogSoftmax often implemented jointly rather than as log(softmax(x)) in separate steps?

options.text: It removes the need for exponentials entirely.
options.explanation: The computation still needs exponentials (inside the log-sum-exp term). The joint form just evaluates them in a numerically safer way.

options.text: It makes the output one-hot.
options.explanation: LogSoftmax produces log-probabilities for all classes, not a one-hot vector. One-hot is a label encoding, not an effect of this layer.

options.text: It guarantees zero loss.
options.explanation: The layer only transforms scores; the loss value still depends on the prediction and the target. Nothing can guarantee zero loss.

options.text: The joint implementation can be more efficient and numerically stable.
options.explanation: Computing $x_i-\log\sum_j e^{x_j}$ with the log-sum-exp trick avoids overflow in $e^{x}$ and the $\log(0)$ that appears when probabilities underflow.

options.text: It changes the mathematical function compared with $\log(\text{softmax}(x))$; the improved stability comes from using a different output.
options.explanation: The joint version computes exactly the same mathematical function. The stability improvement comes from a better way of evaluating it, not from a different result.

hints: What happens to $e^{1000}$ in floating point, and to $\log(0)$?
Simplify $\log\frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}$ analytically.
explanation: Analytically $\log\text{softmax}(x)_i=x_i-\log\sum_j e^{x_j}$. Evaluating softmax first can overflow for large scores or underflow to 0 and then give $\log 0=-\infty$. A fused LogSoftmax subtracts the maximum score before exponentiating (log-sum-exp trick), giving the same function but with stable and cheaper computation.

title: Practical advice for choosing activations
prompt: Which is the commonly recommended practice when choosing an activation function for hidden layers?

options.text: Try ReLU first.
options.explanation: ReLU is cheap, does not saturate for positive inputs and works well in a wide range of networks, so it is the standard first choice before trying variants.

options.text: Sigmoid is always best for deep hidden layers.
options.explanation: Sigmoid saturates and has a derivative of at most 0.25, so deep stacks of sigmoids suffer from vanishing gradients. It is mainly used at outputs for binary probabilities.

options.text: Always mix many activation functions in one network.
options.explanation: There is no benefit in mixing arbitrarily; it only complicates tuning. Usually one activation family is used for the hidden layers.

options.text: There is one clear winner across all networks and datasets.
options.explanation: Which activation works best depends on architecture and data. No single function dominates everywhere, so ReLU variants are tried empirically if the default underperforms.

hints: Which activation avoids saturation on the positive side and is cheap to compute?
Would one function really be optimal for every task?
explanation: The usual guideline is to start with ReLU and only switch to variants (Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU, SELU, ...) if you see problems such as dead units. There is no universal best function, and saturating functions such as sigmoid are poor hidden-layer choices in deep networks.

title: Randomized Leaky ReLU
prompt: Which statement about RReLU is correct?

options.text: During training, its negative-side slope is randomly sampled from a fixed interval rather than learned.
options.explanation: RReLU draws the slope for negative inputs from a uniform distribution over a fixed range during training (and uses a fixed average slope at evaluation), which acts as a regulariser.

options.text: Its positive branch clamps all positive values to 1.
options.explanation: Like ReLU, RReLU is the identity for positive inputs. Clamping at a constant would be a different function (e.g. Hardtanh).

options.text: Its negative-side slope is always exactly zero.
options.explanation: A zero negative slope is plain ReLU. RReLU's randomly sampled slope is nonzero, which keeps a gradient for negative inputs.

options.text: It is identical to PReLU because both learn the slope by gradient descent.
options.explanation: RReLU's slope is sampled at random, not trained by gradient descent. Only PReLU learns its slope.

hints: The first R stands for 'randomized'.
Is the slope updated by the optimiser, or drawn from a distribution?
explanation: RReLU is a Leaky ReLU whose negative slope is drawn at random from a fixed interval in each training pass; at test time a fixed average slope is used. The three variants differ in how the slope is set: fixed (Leaky ReLU), learned (PReLU), randomly sampled (RReLU).

title: Idea behind SELU
prompt: What is the main idea behind SELU?

options.text: Replace every activation with a hard threshold.
options.explanation: A hard threshold has zero gradient almost everywhere and cannot be trained with backpropagation. SELU is a smooth-ish, ELU-like function.

options.text: Use a scaled ELU-like activation as part of a self-normalizing network.
options.explanation: SELU is $\lambda\cdot\text{ELU}$ with fixed constants $\lambda\approx1.0507$ and $\alpha\approx1.6733$, chosen so that activations tend towards zero mean and unit variance from layer to layer.

options.text: Normalize across the minibatch inside the activation function.
options.explanation: SELU is element-wise and uses no batch statistics. Normalising across the minibatch is what batch normalization does as a separate layer.

options.text: Make the negative slope a learned parameter for each neuron.
options.explanation: A learned negative slope is PReLU. SELU's constants are fixed by theory, not trained.

options.text: It computes minibatch mean and variance inside the activation function to obtain self-normalization.
options.explanation: SELU never computes batch statistics. The self-normalising effect comes from the specific scaling constants of the function (together with suitable weight initialisation).

hints: The 'S' stands for 'scaled' and the idea is 'self-normalizing'.
Does SELU need any statistics computed over the batch?
explanation: SELU applies a fixed scaling $\lambda$ to an ELU with a particular $\alpha$. With suitable initialisation, these constants make the mean and variance of activations converge to 0 and 1 across layers, without an explicit normalisation layer. The normalisation is built into the function's shape, not computed from batch statistics.

title: CELU versus ELU on the negative side
prompt: Which statement correctly describes how CELU differs from ELU on the negative branch?

options.text: CELU is simply ReLU clamped at 6.
options.explanation: ReLU clamped at 6 is ReLU6. CELU has an exponential negative branch and no upper clamp.

options.text: CELU has no negative-output region.
options.explanation: For $x<0$ CELU outputs $\alpha(\exp(x/\alpha)-1)<0$, so it does produce negative values, bounded below by $-\alpha$.

options.text: CELU is defined as x times sigmoid(x).
options.explanation: That is the definition of SiLU/Swish. CELU is a rescaled-argument variant of ELU.

options.text: For x < 0, CELU uses $\alpha(\exp(x/\alpha)-1)$, whereas ELU uses $\alpha(\exp(x)-1)$.
options.explanation: CELU divides the exponent's argument by $\alpha$. This makes the derivative at 0 equal to 1 for any $\alpha$, so the function is continuously differentiable.

hints: Compare the exponent in the two negative branches.
Differentiate both negative branches at x = 0 and compare with the slope 1 on the positive side.
explanation: The two functions differ only in the exponent of the negative branch: ELU has $\alpha(e^{x}-1)$ and CELU has $\alpha(e^{x/\alpha}-1)$. For ELU the slope at 0 from the left is $\alpha$, which equals the right slope 1 only if $\alpha=1$; for CELU the left slope is $e^{0}=1$ for every $\alpha$, so it is continuously differentiable.

title: Behaviour of Hardtanh
prompt: Which statement about Hardtanh is correct?

options.text: It is identical to standard tanh at every input.
options.explanation: Hardtanh is a piecewise-linear approximation of tanh. The two agree near 0 only roughly and differ elsewhere (e.g. tanh(0.5) is about 0.46, Hardtanh(0.5) is 0.5).

options.text: It always outputs values in [0, 1].
options.explanation: By default Hardtanh is clamped to [-1, 1], so it can output negative values. A [0, 1] range would be closer to a clipped ReLU.

options.text: It uses a learned slope on negative inputs.
options.explanation: Hardtanh has no trainable parameters; it is a fixed clamp. A learned negative slope is PReLU.

options.text: It behaves linearly between lower and upper bounds and clamps outside them.
options.explanation: $\text{Hardtanh}(x)=\min(\max(x,a),b)$ with default bounds $a=-1$, $b=1$: identity in $[a,b]$ and constant outside.

options.text: It follows the smooth tanh curve between its lower and upper clipping bounds.
options.explanation: Between the bounds, Hardtanh is the straight line $y=x$, not a curve. Only the clipping at the ends resembles tanh's saturation.

hints: The word 'hard' means piecewise linear instead of smooth.
What is Hardtanh(0.5) and Hardtanh(3) with the default bounds?
explanation: Hardtanh is a cheap approximation of tanh: it equals $x$ between a lower and an upper bound (default -1 and 1) and is clamped to those bounds outside. It is not smooth, has no parameters and equals the identity, not the tanh curve, in the middle region.

title: Sigmoid saturation versus ReLU
prompt: Explain why stacking many sigmoid layers makes a network hard to train, and why ReLU (and its leaky variants) helps. Also name the main weakness of plain ReLU and how Leaky ReLU addresses it.
model_answer: The sigmoid derivative $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$ is at most 0.25 and goes to 0 when the unit saturates. Backpropagation multiplies one such factor per layer, so the gradient reaching early layers shrinks exponentially with depth (vanishing gradient). ReLU has derivative exactly 1 for positive inputs, so the gradient passes through active units undiminished, and it is cheap to compute. Its weakness is that units with negative pre-activations have zero gradient and can die; Leaky ReLU keeps a small nonzero slope on the negative side so some gradient always flows.
key_points: The sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25 and tends to 0 when saturated.
Backpropagation multiplies one derivative per layer, so gradients vanish exponentially with depth.
ReLU has gradient 1 for positive inputs, so it does not shrink gradients on active units.
Plain ReLU has zero gradient for negative inputs, so units can die; Leaky ReLU keeps a small nonzero slope there.
hints: Write the gradient through L layers as a product of local derivatives.
What is the derivative of ReLU on each side of zero?
explanation: A complete answer links the maximum value of the sigmoid derivative (0.25) to the product over layers in the chain rule, which gives a factor of at most $0.25^L$. ReLU avoids this because its derivative is 1 on the active side. Common half-answers only say 'sigmoid is slow' without explaining the vanishing product, or forget that ReLU's own problem is the zero gradient for negative inputs (dying ReLU), which Leaky ReLU, PReLU and ELU mitigate.

title: Numerical stability of log-softmax
prompt: Explain what can go wrong if you compute log(softmax(x)) as two separate steps for scores such as x = (1000, 0), and why a fused LogSoftmax avoids this even though it is mathematically the same function.
model_answer: With x = (1000, 0), $e^{1000}$ overflows to infinity in floating point, so softmax gives inf/inf = NaN. For very negative gaps, a probability can underflow to exactly 0 and then $\log 0=-\infty$. The fused version uses $\log\text{softmax}(x)_i=x_i-\log\sum_j e^{x_j}$ and evaluates the log-sum-exp as $m+\log\sum_j e^{x_j-m}$ with $m=\max_j x_j$. All exponents are then at most 0, so nothing overflows, and the log is never applied to zero.
key_points: Exponentiating large scores overflows (inf/inf gives NaN).
Tiny probabilities can underflow to 0 and then the log gives minus infinity.
The fused form uses the identity $\log\text{softmax}(x)_i=x_i-\log\sum_j e^{x_j}$.
Subtracting the maximum score (log-sum-exp trick) keeps all exponents at most 0 without changing the result.
hints: What is $e^{1000}$ in 32-bit floating point?
How can you shift all scores without changing the softmax?
explanation: Softmax is invariant to subtracting a constant from all scores, which is exactly what the log-sum-exp trick exploits: subtract the maximum before exponentiating. The result is mathematically identical, but the computation stays within floating-point range. A frequent wrong answer is that the fused version computes a different function; it does not, it only evaluates it more safely and more cheaply.

title: Identifying an activation from its formula
prompt: Which formula defines the Softsign activation?

options.text: $\log(1+\exp(x))$
options.explanation: This is Softplus, a smooth approximation of ReLU. Its output is always positive and unbounded above, whereas Softsign is odd and bounded in $(-1, 1)$.
Softsign divides the input by $1+|x|$, which squashes it into $(-1, 1)$, is odd like tanh and has derivative $1/(1+|x|)^2$.
For $x>0$ this equals $x$ and for $x<0$ it equals $0.01x$, which is the Leaky ReLU with slope 0.01. It is piecewise linear and unbounded, unlike Softsign.

options.text: $x*\text{sigmoid}(x)$
options.explanation: This is Swish (also called SiLU). It multiplies the input by a sigmoid gate and is unbounded above and non-monotonic, while Softsign is bounded and monotonic.

explanation: Softsign is $f(x) = \frac{x}{1+|x|}$. It behaves like tanh (odd, zero-centred, outputs in $(-1, 1)$) but saturates polynomially instead of exponentially, so its tails decay more slowly. The other formulas are common look-alikes: Softplus, Leaky ReLU and Swish. Match each activation to its defining formula by checking its range and shape.

title: Facts about smooth ReLU-like activations
prompt: Which statement about GELU, Swish or Mish is correct?

options.text: Swish can be written as $x$ multiplied by $\text{sigmoid}(x)$.
options.explanation: Swish (SiLU) is $f(x) = x\,\sigma(x)$, a smooth gate that lets large positive inputs pass and suppresses large negative ones.

options.text: Mish is defined as $\max(0, x)$.
options.explanation: $\max(0, x)$ is plain ReLU. Mish is the smooth function $x \tanh(\text{softplus}(x))$, which is differentiable everywhere.

options.text: Swish is a strictly monotonic activation.
options.explanation: Swish is non-monotonic: it dips to a minimum of about $-0.28$ near $x \approx -1.28$ and then rises again. Smooth ReLU variants such as GELU and Mish share this small negative dip.

options.text: GELU is a piecewise-constant function.
options.explanation: GELU is $x\,\Phi(x)$ with $\Phi$ the Gaussian CDF, a smooth, continuous, non-constant curve. A piecewise-constant function would have zero gradient almost everywhere and could not be trained with backpropagation.

explanation: GELU, Swish and Mish are smooth, non-monotonic relatives of ReLU that all take the form of the input times a smooth gate: $x\,\Phi(x)$, $x\,\sigma(x)$ and $x \tanh(\text{softplus}(x))$. They are close to the identity for large positive inputs and close to zero for large negative ones, with a small negative dip in between. Remember that being smooth and having a dip are the key differences from ReLU.

title: ReLU derivative at the kink
prompt: How is a software implementation expected to handle ReLU at $x = 0$, where the ordinary derivative does not exist?

options.text: Replace the ReLU by a sigmoid only during the backward pass.
options.explanation: The backward pass must be the derivative of the same function used in the forward pass. Swapping in a sigmoid would give gradients of a different function and is never done.

options.text: Always return an infinite derivative.
options.explanation: ReLU has slope 0 on the left and 1 on the right, so every one-sided derivative and subgradient is finite, in $[0, 1]$. An infinite value would make the gradients explode.

options.text: Declare backpropagation impossible for any network containing ReLU.
options.explanation: Backpropagation works fine with ReLU. Exactly $x = 0$ is a single point that is hit with probability close to zero for real-valued inputs, and any valid choice there is acceptable.

options.text: Use a valid convention such as the left derivative, right derivative, or a subgradient choice.
options.explanation: At $x = 0$ any value in $[0, 1]$ is a valid subgradient, and the left derivative (0) or right derivative (1) are special cases. Frameworks pick one, typically 0.

explanation: ReLU is convex and piecewise linear, so at its kink it has a subdifferential equal to the interval $[0, 1]$ instead of a single derivative. Implementations simply pick a value from it (PyTorch uses 0), which is a legitimate subgradient. Because the kink is hit with essentially zero probability and the choice is valid, training is unaffected in practice.

title: Choosing an activation function
prompt: Which statements about choosing activation functions in practice are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The best activation is independent of all other network components.
options.explanation: The best choice depends on the rest of the setup (architecture, optimizer, initialization, data). An activation that works well in one setting can fail in another, so it has to be tuned together with them.

options.text: Mixing many activation-function types inside one network is recommended as the default.
options.explanation: The usual recommendation is the opposite: use one well-understood activation consistently and deviate only when there is a reason. Mixing many types adds hyperparameters and makes the model harder to analyse without a reliable gain.

options.text: There is no clear universal winner across all tasks and architectures.
options.explanation: Empirical comparisons show that the ranking of activations changes with task and architecture. Differences between good activations are often small compared to other design choices.

options.text: ReLU is a reasonable first activation to try.
options.explanation: ReLU is cheap, simple and works well in many networks, so it is a sensible baseline before trying GELU, Swish or others.

options.text: Activation choice interacts with optimizer, learning rate, depth, data and initialization.
options.explanation: For example, ReLU needs a He-style initialization to keep variances stable, and saturating activations make deep networks hard to train with plain SGD. Activation choice cannot be judged in isolation.

explanation: There is no universally best activation. A good practice is to start from a simple default such as ReLU and then try alternatives, remembering that their effect is entangled with initialization, optimizer, learning rate, depth and data. Treat the activation as one part of a whole training recipe.

title: What a normalization layer does
prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of a normalization layer?

options.text: Replace the loss function.
options.explanation: Normalization layers sit inside the network and transform activations. The loss function is a separate component that compares outputs with targets.

options.text: Change the number of samples in a minibatch.
options.explanation: Normalization keeps the tensor shape unchanged, including the batch size. The batch size is a data-loading choice, although BatchNorm statistics do depend on it.

options.text: Increase the spatial resolution of a feature map.
options.explanation: Increasing resolution is done by upsampling or transposed convolution. Normalization preserves height and width.

options.text: Control statistics such as the mean and variance of values in a tensor.
options.explanation: Normalization layers subtract a mean and divide by a standard deviation (or RMS) over some set of axes, usually followed by a learnable scale and shift. This keeps activations in a well-behaved range and eases optimization.

explanation: A normalization layer rescales its input so that selected statistics, typically mean and variance, are controlled over a chosen set of axes. The different variants (Batch, Layer, Instance, Group, RMS) differ only in which axes they aggregate over. It never changes the tensor's shape.

title: Axes of spatial BatchNorm
prompt: For spatial BatchNorm on an $N \times C \times H \times W$ tensor, which set of axes is aggregated to compute each channel's statistics?

options.text: $N$ and $C$ only
options.explanation: The channel axis $C$ is the one kept, not aggregated: there is one mean and variance per channel. Also, the spatial axes $H$ and $W$ must be included in the average.

options.text: $C$ only
options.explanation: Averaging over $C$ would mix different channels into one statistic, and it would not use the batch. BatchNorm gives each channel its own statistics.

options.text: $H$ and $W$ only, excluding $N$
options.explanation: Averaging over just the spatial positions of each sample, per channel, is Instance Normalization. BatchNorm also averages across the $N$ samples.

options.text: $N$, $H$ and $W$
options.explanation: For each channel $c$ the mean and variance are taken over all $N \cdot H \cdot W$ values of that channel, giving $C$ means and $C$ variances.

explanation: Spatial BatchNorm treats every pixel of every sample as one observation of its channel, so statistics are computed over $(N, H, W)$ and there are $C$ means, variances and $\gamma, \beta$ pairs. The comparison is: BatchNorm aggregates over $(N, H, W)$, Instance Norm over $(H, W)$, Layer Norm over $(C, H, W)$.

title: BatchNorm for vector inputs
prompt: Which statements about BatchNorm for vectors (an $N \times D$ input) are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It computes one mean and one variance per feature.
options.explanation: For each of the $D$ features, the mean and variance are taken over the $N$ samples of the minibatch, giving $D$ means and $D$ variances.

options.text: Its training statistics are computed independently for each sample rather than across the minibatch.
options.explanation: This describes LayerNorm. BatchNorm's statistics are computed across the minibatch, so one sample's output depends on the other samples in the batch.

options.text: It removes all learnable parameters from the normalization layer.
options.explanation: BatchNorm keeps a learnable scale $\gamma$ and shift $\beta$ per feature, so that the network can recover any mean and variance it needs (including undoing the normalization).

options.text: It uses one single scalar mean for the entire $N \times D$ matrix.
options.explanation: A single global mean would ignore that features have different scales. BatchNorm normalizes each of the $D$ features with its own mean and variance.

options.text: It learns a scale $\gamma$ and shift $\beta$ per feature.
options.explanation: After normalizing, the output is $\gamma_d \hat{x}_d + \beta_d$, with $2D$ learnable parameters in total.

options.text: During training, its mean and variance depend on the current minibatch.
options.explanation: Training uses the statistics of the current minibatch (and updates running averages for later). This makes the output of a sample depend on its batchmates and adds some noise.

explanation: BatchNorm for vectors normalizes each feature (column of the $N \times D$ matrix) using the minibatch mean and variance, then applies a per-feature learnable scale and shift. During training the statistics come from the current minibatch, which is why output depends on batch composition and why test time needs a different rule. Do not confuse it with LayerNorm, which averages over the features of each sample.

title: BatchNorm at test time
prompt: What statistics does BatchNorm use at test time?

options.text: Statistics computed only from the current single test example.
options.explanation: With one example the per-feature variance over the batch would be undefined (or zero), and predictions would depend on whatever is in the batch. Test-time outputs should be deterministic per sample.

options.text: Running estimates of mean and variance accumulated during training.
options.explanation: During training the layer keeps an exponential moving average of the minibatch means and variances. At test time these fixed values are used, so the layer becomes a fixed affine transform per feature.

options.text: The gradients from the previous minibatch.
options.explanation: Gradients are used to update weights in training and play no role in the forward normalization. Normalization uses means and variances of activations.

options.text: The training labels.
options.explanation: BatchNorm never uses labels, and labels are not available at test time anyway. It only uses statistics of the activations.

explanation: BatchNorm cannot use minibatch statistics at test time, since predictions should not depend on other test samples and a batch may even contain a single example. Instead it uses running averages of mean and variance gathered during training. This is why a model must be switched between train and eval mode, and why BatchNorm behaves differently in the two modes.

title: Bias before BatchNorm
prompt: Why is a bias often unnecessary in a convolution or linear layer immediately followed by BatchNorm?

options.text: BatchNorm makes all weights equal to zero.
options.explanation: BatchNorm does not touch the weights of the preceding layer; it only rescales its outputs, and the weights keep learning normally.

options.text: The bias would change the spatial resolution.
options.explanation: A bias is a per-channel constant added to the output, so it never changes height or width. Resolution is set by kernel size, stride and padding.

options.text: PyTorch does not allow bias together with BatchNorm.
options.explanation: PyTorch allows it. It is only redundant, so people set `bias=False` to save a few parameters.

options.text: Subtracting the BatchNorm mean removes the constant bias contribution, and beta provides a learnable shift.
options.explanation: If the layer outputs $z + b$, the batch mean is $\bar{z} + b$ and the centred value is $(z + b) - (\bar{z} + b) = z - \bar{z}$, so $b$ cancels exactly. The learnable $\beta$ then supplies the shift.

options.text: The preceding bias is redundant because BatchNorm's learned scale $\gamma$ absorbs the bias.
options.explanation: The scale $\gamma$ multiplies the normalized values and cannot add a constant. The redundancy is caused by mean subtraction, which cancels the bias, with $\beta$ taking over the role of the shift.

explanation: BatchNorm first subtracts the per-feature (per-channel) batch mean. A constant per-feature bias added by the preceding layer shifts the mean by exactly the same amount, so it cancels out and has no effect on the output. The only offset that survives is the learnable $\beta$ of BatchNorm itself, so the previous bias just wastes parameters.

title: Where BatchNorm is placed
prompt: In the original BatchNorm formulation, where is BatchNorm placed relative to the linear/conv layer and activation?

options.text: BatchNorm placement is fixed identically for every architecture.
options.explanation: Only the original formulation fixes the order. Later work often places it after the activation or elsewhere (for example in residual blocks), so placement is a design choice that varies between architectures.

options.text: BatchNorm must always be placed after dropout and never near a convolution.
options.explanation: BatchNorm is used right after convolutions in most CNNs. There is no rule forcing it after dropout; in fact, dropout and BatchNorm interact poorly.

options.text: The original formulation places BatchNorm after a linear/conv layer and before the nonlinearity.
options.explanation: The original pattern is Linear/Conv, then BatchNorm, then activation (for example ReLU), so that the pre-activations are normalized.

options.text: BatchNorm must always be placed both before and after every nonlinearity.
options.explanation: One BatchNorm per layer is the standard pattern. Adding one both before and after every nonlinearity would double the cost and is not what the method prescribes.

explanation: In the original paper the block is Conv/Linear, BatchNorm, nonlinearity. This normalizes the pre-activations, and it is also why the preceding layer's bias becomes unnecessary. Variants with BatchNorm after the activation exist, so treat the original order as the baseline and not as a law.

title: LayerNorm versus BatchNorm
prompt: Which statements correctly compare LayerNorm with BatchNorm for a batch of vectors? (Select all that apply)

options.text: LayerNorm requires running averages at test time.
options.explanation: LayerNorm computes statistics from the current sample itself, so it has no running averages. It is BatchNorm that needs them for inference.

options.text: LayerNorm has the same behavior during training and testing, whereas BatchNorm uses batch-dependent statistics during training.
options.explanation: LayerNorm's computation depends only on the sample, so train and eval are identical. BatchNorm switches from minibatch statistics to running estimates.

options.text: BatchNorm statistics depend only on a single sample.
options.explanation: BatchNorm's statistics are averages over the whole minibatch (per feature), so every sample's output depends on the others. Dependence on a single sample is a property of LayerNorm.

options.text: LayerNorm always changes the tensor shape.
options.explanation: LayerNorm is shape preserving, like all normalization layers. It only changes the values.

options.text: LayerNorm computes statistics within each sample, whereas BatchNorm aggregates across the batch.
options.explanation: For an $N \times D$ input, LayerNorm takes a mean and variance over the $D$ features of each row, while BatchNorm takes them over the $N$ samples of each column.

explanation: The two layers differ in the axis they average over: BatchNorm over the batch (per feature), LayerNorm over the features (per sample). As a consequence LayerNorm is independent of other samples, needs no running averages and behaves identically in training and inference. Both layers keep the input shape.

title: Properties of LayerNorm
prompt: Which statements about LayerNorm are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It does not require a batch of samples to compute its statistics.
options.explanation: The mean and variance are computed over the features of one sample, so even a batch of size 1 works.

options.text: It can behave the same during training and testing.
options.explanation: Since the statistics come only from the current sample, no running averages are needed and the train and test computation is identical.

options.text: It cannot be applied to vector inputs.
options.explanation: Vectors are the standard case: for a vector of $D$ features, the layer normalizes its entries with their mean and variance. Transformers apply LayerNorm to token vectors.

options.text: Its statistics must always be computed across the batch dimension.
options.explanation: Statistics across the batch define BatchNorm. LayerNorm aggregates over feature dimensions within each sample, not across the batch.

options.text: It is useful in settings where batch-dependent statistics are unattractive.
options.explanation: Examples are tiny batches, variable-length sequences or autoregressive inference with a single token, where batch statistics would be noisy or ill-defined.

explanation: LayerNorm normalizes within each sample, so it does not depend on the batch, needs no running estimates and is identical at training and test time. This makes it a natural fit for sequence models and transformers, where batch statistics are awkward. The statistics are taken over features, never over the batch.

title: Properties of RMSNorm
prompt: Which statements about RMSNorm are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It necessarily includes a learned shift $\beta$ in the formulation shown.
options.explanation: The usual RMSNorm is $y = \frac{x}{\text{RMS}(x)} \odot g$ with only a learned gain $g$. A shift is not part of the method, which is one way it is cheaper than LayerNorm.

options.text: It is independent of the batch dimension.
options.explanation: Its statistic is computed only from the entries of a single sample, so other samples in the batch have no influence.

options.text: It requires running mean and variance estimates for inference.
options.explanation: Because it uses only the current sample, it has no running estimates, and train and inference behave identically.

options.text: It uses a root-mean-square statistic for each sample.
options.explanation: It divides by $\text{RMS}(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{D}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}$, computed over the features of each sample.

options.text: It always subtracts the sample mean before rescaling.
options.explanation: Mean subtraction is what LayerNorm does. RMSNorm skips the centring step and only rescales by the root mean square.

explanation: RMSNorm is a simplified LayerNorm: it drops the mean subtraction (and typically the bias) and only rescales each sample by its root mean square, $x / \sqrt{\frac{1}{D}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}$, then multiplies by a learned gain. Being per-sample, it is batch independent and has no running statistics. It is cheaper than LayerNorm and common in modern transformers.

title: Pre-norm versus post-norm transformer blocks
prompt: Which statement correctly compares pre-norm and post-norm transformer blocks?

options.text: Post-norm applies normalization only to the model input before all layers.
options.explanation: Post-norm applies normalization in every block, after the sublayer and the residual addition, not once on the model input.

options.text: Pre-norm requires BatchNorm statistics across the minibatch.
options.explanation: Pre-norm only says where the normalization sits. Transformers typically use LayerNorm or RMSNorm there, which need no minibatch statistics.

options.text: Pre-norm applies normalization before the sublayer and keeps a clean residual path.
options.explanation: A pre-norm block computes $x + F(\text{Norm}(x))$, so the identity path from input to output is untouched by normalization, which helps gradient flow in deep stacks.

options.text: Post-norm removes the residual connection.
options.explanation: Post-norm keeps the residual connection: it computes $\text{Norm}(x + F(x))$. The difference is that the sum goes through the normalization.

options.text: In pre-norm, normalization is applied only after the sublayer output has been added to the residual connection.
options.explanation: That describes post-norm. In pre-norm, the normalization is applied to the sublayer's input, and the sublayer output is added to the unnormalized residual stream.

explanation: Post-norm computes $\text{Norm}(x + F(x))$, so every layer's output, including the residual path, passes through a normalization. Pre-norm computes $x + F(\text{Norm}(x))$, which leaves a clean identity path and tends to make deep transformers easier and more stable to train. Both keep the residual connection.

title: Purpose of QK-Norm
prompt: What is the purpose of QK-Norm in modern transformers?

options.text: Replace attention with a convolution.
options.explanation: QK-Norm keeps the attention mechanism and only adds a normalization inside it. It does not swap in a convolution.

options.text: Compute running batch statistics for token positions.
options.explanation: QK-Norm is typically a per-vector LayerNorm or RMSNorm and does not use batch statistics or running averages.

options.text: Normalize queries and keys to control the magnitude of attention logits and improve training stability at scale.
options.explanation: Normalizing $Q$ and $K$ bounds the dot products $QK^\top$, which prevents very large logits that saturate the softmax and destabilize training in large models.

options.text: Normalize class labels before the loss.
options.explanation: Labels are targets and are not part of the attention computation. QK-Norm acts on intermediate query and key vectors.

options.text: Normalize only the value vectors $V$ while leaving the queries $Q$ and keys $K$ unchanged.
options.explanation: The logits are $QK^\top$, so only normalizing $Q$ and $K$ controls their size. Normalizing $V$ does not affect the logits at all.

explanation: Attention logits are the dot products $QK^\top / \sqrt{d}$. If queries and keys grow large during training, the softmax becomes extremely peaked and gradients get unstable. QK-Norm normalizes $Q$ and $K$ (usually per head) before the dot product, which bounds the logit magnitude.

title: Instance Normalization on images
prompt: Which statement correctly describes Instance Normalization for image tensors?

options.text: It aggregates over the minibatch dimension exactly like BatchNorm.
options.explanation: Instance Norm does not use the batch dimension at all. Each sample is normalized independently, unlike BatchNorm, which averages over $N$.

options.text: It always uses running statistics at test time.
options.explanation: Because its statistics come from the sample itself, it needs no running averages and can compute them at test time as well. Only BatchNorm requires running statistics at inference.

options.text: It computes one statistic for the entire batch and all channels.
options.explanation: That would be a single global mean and variance. Instance Norm uses a separate statistic for every channel of every sample.

options.text: It computes one mean and variance per channel and per sample over the spatial dimensions.
options.explanation: For an $N \times C \times H \times W$ input, each of the $N \cdot C$ slices has its own mean and variance computed over its $H \cdot W$ pixels.

explanation: Instance Norm normalizes each (sample, channel) slice over its spatial positions, so it aggregates over $(H, W)$ only. It therefore does not depend on the batch and behaves the same in training and test, which is why it is popular in style transfer and image generation.

title: Group Normalization details
prompt: Which statements about Group Normalization are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Its statistics must aggregate over the minibatch axis.
options.explanation: Group Norm computes statistics per sample, so it never averages over the batch. This is its main advantage over BatchNorm.

options.text: It changes the spatial height and width of the tensor.
options.explanation: Like every normalization layer it preserves the shape of the input; only the values are rescaled.

options.text: It normalizes over channels within each group and over spatial dimensions.
options.explanation: For each sample and each group, the mean and variance are computed over the $C/G$ channels of that group and all $H \times W$ positions.

options.text: The number of groups $G$ may be any real-valued number.
options.explanation: $G$ is a positive integer hyperparameter, since it counts groups of channels. A non-integer number of groups makes no sense.

options.text: $G$ must divide the number of channels.
options.explanation: The $C$ channels are split into $G$ equal groups of $C/G$ channels, so $C$ must be divisible by $G$.

options.text: It splits the channels into $G$ groups.
options.explanation: This is its defining step: the channel axis is divided into $G$ groups and each group is normalized separately.

explanation: Group Norm splits the $C$ channels into $G$ groups (so $G$ must be an integer that divides $C$) and normalizes each group of each sample over its channels and spatial positions. It sits between Instance Norm ($G = C$) and LayerNorm ($G = 1$). It never uses the batch axis, and it preserves the tensor shape.

title: GroupNorm with tiny batches
prompt: Why is GroupNorm often useful when per-device batch sizes are very small?

options.text: It estimates running statistics from the test set.
options.explanation: Using the test set for statistics would be a form of leakage, and GroupNorm needs no running statistics at all.

options.text: It increases the physical batch size automatically.
options.explanation: GroupNorm does not change the batch size. It is simply insensitive to it.

options.text: It removes all convolutional parameters.
options.explanation: The convolutions keep all their weights. GroupNorm adds only a small per-channel scale and shift.

options.text: Its statistics do not aggregate over the batch dimension, so they are not degraded by tiny minibatches.
options.explanation: Mean and variance are computed per sample from groups of channels, so they are as accurate with a batch of 1 or 2 as with a batch of 64.

explanation: BatchNorm estimates statistics from the minibatch, so very small batches (common with large images or detection and segmentation models) give noisy estimates and hurt performance. GroupNorm computes statistics inside each sample, so its quality does not depend on batch size. It is a standard replacement when batches are tiny.

title: Per-pixel feature normalization
prompt: Per-pixel normalization (as in PixelNorm) rescales the channel vector at every spatial location of a feature map. Which statements about it are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It aggregates statistics across the whole minibatch.
options.explanation: Each pixel's channel vector is normalized on its own, so nothing is averaged across the batch.

options.text: Each spatial pixel vector is rescaled using its own channel-wise length or RMS.
options.explanation: At every position $(h, w)$, the $C$-dimensional vector is divided by $\sqrt{\frac{1}{C}\sum_c x_c^2 + \epsilon}$, computed from that vector alone.

options.text: It changes the spatial resolution of the feature map.
options.explanation: It rescales values at each pixel and keeps $H$ and $W$ unchanged, like every normalization layer.

options.text: It requires running statistics for test-time inference.
options.explanation: Since the statistic is computed from the current pixel vector, nothing needs to be accumulated during training and the layer behaves the same at test time.

options.text: It does not subtract a mean.
options.explanation: It only divides by the RMS (the vector's scaled length). There is no centring step, so it is like RMSNorm applied across channels at each pixel.

explanation: Per-pixel normalization treats the channel vector at each location as the unit to normalize and divides it by its RMS, with no mean subtraction. It therefore works without batch statistics or running averages, and does not alter the tensor shape. Compare it with RMSNorm, which has the same formula over a different set of entries.

title: What spectral normalization acts on
prompt: What does spectral normalization normalize?

options.text: The weights of a layer using the largest singular value of the weight matrix.
options.explanation: The weight is replaced by $W / \sigma_{\max}(W)$, so the layer's spectral norm becomes 1, which bounds how much the layer can stretch its inputs.

options.text: The activations of each minibatch to zero mean and unit variance.
options.explanation: That is BatchNorm, which acts on activations. Spectral normalization acts on weights and does not use minibatch statistics.

options.text: The class probabilities after softmax.
options.explanation: Softmax outputs already sum to 1 and are not related to a weight's singular values. Spectral normalization is applied to the weights.

options.text: Only the bias vector of a layer.
options.explanation: The bias is not touched. The scaling is computed from the weight matrix, as bias terms do not affect the Lipschitz constant of the layer.

explanation: Spectral normalization divides a layer's weight matrix by its largest singular value (usually estimated by power iteration), so the layer is 1-Lipschitz. It is used for example in GAN discriminators to stabilize training. It is a weight reparametrization, not a normalization of activations.

title: BatchNorm versus LayerNorm in training and inference
prompt: Explain why BatchNorm must behave differently at training and test time while LayerNorm does not. Then explain why LayerNorm is the safer choice when the batch is tiny or when sequences are processed one token at a time.
model_answer: BatchNorm normalizes each feature using the mean and variance over the minibatch, so its output depends on the other samples in the batch. At test time we want deterministic predictions for each sample, even for a batch of one, so it switches to running averages of mean and variance collected during training. LayerNorm computes the mean and variance over the features of each sample alone, so train and test are identical and no running averages are needed. With tiny batches the BatchNorm estimates become noisy (and are undefined for a single sample), whereas LayerNorm quality is independent of the batch size.
key_points: BatchNorm statistics are computed across the minibatch, so a sample's output depends on the other samples.
At test time BatchNorm uses running averages accumulated during training.
LayerNorm computes statistics within each sample, so train and test behaviour are identical and there are no running statistics.
Small batches give noisy BatchNorm estimates, while LayerNorm is unaffected by batch size.
explanation: The central idea is the axis of aggregation: batch axis for BatchNorm, feature axis for LayerNorm. Everything else follows from it, including running averages, the train/eval switch and sensitivity to batch size. A common half-answer only says that LayerNorm is used in transformers without explaining the dependence on other samples. Another mistake is to say that BatchNorm uses the test batch's statistics, which would make a prediction depend on its batchmates.

title: Why pre-norm blocks train more easily
prompt: Compare a post-norm block $\text{Norm}(x + F(x))$ with a pre-norm block $x + F(\text{Norm}(x))$ in a deep transformer. Explain why the pre-norm variant is usually easier to train.
model_answer: In a post-norm block the residual sum passes through a normalization, so the identity path from the input to the output is repeatedly transformed. The gradient flowing to early layers must pass through every normalization of the stack, which can make training unstable in deep models and often requires learning-rate warm-up. In a pre-norm block the normalization is applied only to the input of the sublayer, so the residual path is a clean identity: the output is the input plus a correction. Gradients can flow directly from the loss to early layers through the identity connection, which makes deep stacks more stable to train.
key_points: Post-norm normalizes after the residual addition, so the skip path itself goes through a normalization in each block.
Pre-norm normalizes only the sublayer input, leaving the residual stream as an untouched identity path.
The clean identity path lets gradients reach early layers directly, giving more stable training of deep models.
Post-norm gradients must pass through many normalizations, so it is more sensitive and often needs warm-up.
explanation: The key is the residual connection: its value is that it provides a direct gradient route, and post-norm partly spoils it by putting a normalization on that route. A half-answer only says that pre-norm is more stable without naming the clean residual path. A common mistake is to claim that post-norm removes the residual connection, which it does not. A further caveat is that the pre-norm residual stream can grow with depth, so a final normalization is usually added before the output layer.

title: Spectral normalization facts
prompt: Which statements about spectral normalization are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Dividing the weight matrix by its largest singular value can make the linear map 1-Lipschitz.
options.explanation: After the division, $W/\sigma_{\max}(W)$ has spectral norm 1, so $\|Wx - Wy\| \le \|x - y\|$ for all inputs: the map cannot expand distances, which is exactly 1-Lipschitz.

options.text: The spectral norm of a matrix is the largest singular value of the weight matrix.
options.explanation: The spectral (operator 2-) norm $\|W\|_2 = \max_{x\neq 0}\|Wx\|/\|x\|$ equals the largest singular value $\sigma_{\max}(W)$.

options.text: It requires learnable gamma and beta parameters.
options.explanation: Learnable scale (gamma) and shift (beta) belong to batch/layer normalization. Spectral normalization only rescales the weights by a computed constant and adds no learnable parameters.

options.text: Power iteration can approximate the largest singular value more cheaply than running a full SVD at every step.
options.explanation: Power iteration only needs a few matrix-vector products with $W$ and $W^\top$ per training step, which is far cheaper than a full SVD, and the vectors can be reused between steps.

options.text: It uses different formulas during training and testing because of running activation statistics.
options.explanation: Running activation statistics are a batch normalization feature. Spectral normalization depends only on the weights, so it is the same computation in training and testing.

hints: Think about what quantity bounds how much a matrix can stretch a vector.
Which of these properties belong to batch normalization instead (learnable parameters, running statistics)?
explanation: Spectral normalization is a weight normalization: it divides a weight matrix by its spectral norm (largest singular value), which caps how much the layer can stretch its input and makes it 1-Lipschitz. Because it only involves the weights, it has no learnable gamma/beta and no running statistics, which are features of batch normalization. A full SVD would be expensive, so the largest singular value is estimated with cheap power iteration.

title: Reading and comparing architectures
prompt: Which statements about evaluating and reading neural-network architectures are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A model with fewer parameters must always have lower latency.
options.explanation: Latency depends on compute (FLOPs), memory traffic and parallelism, not only on parameter count. For example, convolutions applied to large feature maps reuse few weights many times, so a small model can still be slow.

options.text: Parameter count is a proxy for model size, but it is not the same as compute or latency.
options.explanation: Parameters measure memory for the weights; compute (multiply-adds per forward pass) and latency also depend on feature-map sizes, layer types and hardware.

options.text: Pooling layers are counted toward depth by every author without exception.
options.explanation: Authors differ: depth is often defined as the number of layers with learnable weights, in which case pooling is not counted. Saying 'every author without exception' is false.

options.text: Top-1 accuracy is the fraction of images for which any one of the top five predictions is correct.
options.explanation: That definition is top-5 accuracy. Top-1 accuracy counts an image as correct only if the single highest-scoring class is the true label.

options.text: In the convention used in this course, convolutional and fully connected layers count toward depth, while activations and normalization layers do not.
options.explanation: Depth counts the main weight layers (convolutional and fully connected), e.g. VGG-16 = 13 conv + 3 FC; activations, pooling and normalization layers are not counted.

hints: Is memory for weights the same as the amount of arithmetic performed?
Compare the definitions of top-1 and top-5 accuracy carefully.
explanation: Parameter count, FLOPs and latency measure different things: a model can have few parameters but expensive computation because its weights are reused over large feature maps. Depth is a convention, not a law; the common one counts only conv and fully connected layers, so names like VGG-16 refer to weight layers. Top-1 accuracy requires the single best prediction to be right, while top-5 allows five guesses.

title: Branching computational graphs
prompt: Which statement about branching computational graphs is correct?

options.text: Elementwise addition without broadcasting requires the input tensors to have the same shape.
options.explanation: Elementwise addition pairs entry $i$ of one tensor with entry $i$ of the other, so without broadcasting every dimension must match.

options.text: Copying a tensor changes its values before the branches use it.
options.explanation: A copy (fan-out) sends identical values to every branch; it only duplicates the tensor. In backpropagation the gradients from the branches are summed.

options.text: A chain topology necessarily contains at least one branch point.
options.explanation: A chain is a sequence in which every layer has exactly one input and one output, so by definition it has no branch points.

options.text: Concatenation along the channel dimension requires all input tensors to have the same channel count.
options.explanation: Concatenation requires matching batch and spatial sizes, but the channel counts may differ; the output channel count is their sum.

options.text: Concatenation along the channel dimension adds corresponding channel values elementwise.
options.explanation: That describes addition. Concatenation stacks the tensors next to each other along the channel axis without changing any values, so channels add up in number, not in value.

hints: Compare what addition and concatenation each do to the shape of the result.
What shapes must agree for an elementwise operation?
explanation: Addition merges tensors value by value, so shapes must be identical (without broadcasting) and the output has the same shape. Concatenation joins tensors along one axis, so all other axes must match, while the joined axis may differ and grows to the sum. A copy simply duplicates a tensor for several branches, and a chain has no branching at all.

title: LeNet-5 and AlexNet design choices
prompt: Which statements about LeNet-5 or AlexNet are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: AlexNet's classifier contains no fully connected layers.
options.explanation: AlexNet ends with three fully connected layers (4096, 4096 and 1000 units). Removing fully connected layers is a later trend (global average pooling in Network in Network and GoogLeNet).

options.text: AlexNet begins with an 11 x 11 convolution with stride 4 for aggressive early downsampling.
options.explanation: The first AlexNet layer uses large 11x11 filters with stride 4, which quickly reduces the spatial size of the large input image.

options.text: LeNet-5 uses only max pooling rather than average pooling.
options.explanation: LeNet-5 uses average-style subsampling layers; max pooling became the common choice in later networks such as AlexNet and VGG.

options.text: AlexNet uses ReLU activations as an engineering choice for faster training.
options.explanation: ReLU does not saturate for positive inputs, so gradients flow better and training converges much faster than with tanh or sigmoid.

options.text: LeNet-5 uses ReLU throughout instead of tanh.
options.explanation: LeNet-5 predates the popularity of ReLU and uses saturating activations such as tanh/sigmoid. ReLU is associated with AlexNet.

hints: LeNet-5 is the older network (1990s); which activation and pooling were popular then?
What does AlexNet do at the top of the network, and what does it do at the end?
explanation: LeNet-5 reflects 1990s practice: tanh-like activations and average-pooling (subsampling). AlexNet modernised the recipe with ReLU for faster training, max pooling, a large 11x11 stride-4 first convolution and, still, three fully connected layers at the end. Remembering which design element belongs to which network is the key to this question.

title: VGG and Network in Network
prompt: Which statement about VGG or Network in Network is correct?

options.text: Network in Network removes all 1 x 1 convolutions from the model.
options.explanation: Network in Network is the architecture that popularised 1x1 convolutions: they implement the small per-pixel MLP in each mlpconv block.

options.text: VGG doubles spatial resolution after each max-pooling layer.
options.explanation: Max pooling halves the spatial resolution. What VGG doubles is the number of channels from one stage to the next (64, 128, 256, 512).

options.text: VGG-16 contains 13 convolutional and 3 fully connected weight layers.
options.explanation: VGG-16 has 13 convolutional layers (3x3) and 3 fully connected layers, which gives the 16 weight layers in its name.

options.text: VGG is built mainly from parallel branches using 1 x 1, 3 x 3, and 5 x 5 filters.
options.explanation: That describes the Inception module. VGG is a plain chain of stacked 3x3 convolutions and max pooling with no parallel branches.

options.text: The mlpconv block in Network in Network replaces its local 1×1 transformations with pooling operations.
options.explanation: An mlpconv block is a spatial convolution followed by 1x1 convolutions (a per-pixel MLP). Pooling is not used in place of them; Network in Network uses global average pooling only at the end.

hints: Count the weight layers in VGG-16: the number in the name is the answer.
Which architecture is a plain chain, and which uses parallel branches?
explanation: VGG is a deep plain chain of 3x3 convolutions and max pooling; the 16 in VGG-16 counts 13 conv plus 3 fully connected layers, and channels double between stages while pooling halves the spatial size. Network in Network instead builds mlpconv blocks from a convolution followed by 1x1 convolutions, and replaces the big fully connected head by global average pooling.

title: Inception v1 / GoogLeNet
prompt: Which statements about Inception v1 / GoogLeNet are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: GoogLeNet contains no auxiliary classifiers.
options.explanation: GoogLeNet has two auxiliary classifiers attached to intermediate layers during training. They inject extra gradient and act as regularization, and are discarded at test time.

options.text: The 1 x 1 convolutions are used to increase channels before every expensive convolution.
options.explanation: The 1x1 convolutions are used to reduce the channel count before the 3x3 and 5x5 convolutions (a bottleneck), which lowers computation, not to increase it.

options.text: Inception modules process the same input through parallel branches and concatenate the branch outputs.
options.explanation: An Inception module applies 1x1, 3x3, 5x5 convolutions and pooling in parallel to the same input and concatenates the results along the channel axis.

options.text: GoogLeNet replaces global average pooling with a large stack of fully connected layers.
options.explanation: It is the opposite: GoogLeNet uses global average pooling before a single classifier layer, which removes most of the parameters of large fully connected heads.

options.text: The reduced Inception module uses 1×1 convolutions to reduce channel count before the expensive 3×3 and 5×5 convolutions.
options.explanation: The 1x1 bottleneck shrinks the number of input channels, so the cost of the following 3x3 and 5x5 convolutions drops sharply.

hints: Is a bottleneck meant to make the following layers cheaper or more expensive?
